# Execution Harnesses and Tool Isolation {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

::: {.epigraph}
> "We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."
>
> — John M. Culkin, "A Schoolman's Guide to Marshall McLuhan" [@Culkin1967Schoolman, p. 70]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What is an architecture design environment, and what must it provide for AI-native work?*

**Core thesis:** *An environment is not a simulator wrapper; it coordinates state, tools, workloads, interfaces, failure handling, and multi-fidelity execution to enable closed-loop automated design.*
:::

A tool command is not an environment. An architect can launch a simulator, compiler, formal engine, or physical-design flow and still be unable to say which candidate ran, which state the tool inherited, what an unfamiliar warning meant, or whether a retry repeated the same work. Generative models and automated optimizers widen that gap, because they can propose candidates far faster than tools can evaluate them, and every proposal becomes a run that shares licenses, scratch storage, and compute with the others. On a shared cluster, tool state can be corrupted, license servers can run out of available checkouts, intermediate checkpoints can fill scratch storage, and a generated Tcl script can attempt arbitrary system calls. An execution environment contains each run and binds every returned metric to the recorded inputs, tool versions, and operating conditions that produced it.

Wrappers, harnesses, and isolated execution boundaries assemble that environment (@fig-ch06-cover-map): whereas setup establishes immutable inputs, typed interfaces, and lineage, runtime manages concurrent dispatch, license contention, checkpoint recovery, and error containment. The prospective Lighthouse mobile extended-reality (XR) system-on-chip (SoC) study grounds these responsibilities across several tool interfaces, since its analytical static random-access memory (SRAM) screen is run with a real model while its later execution steps are hypothetical and have not been dispatched. Because the environment determines what executed, what failed, and what returned, what those observations support and how they should steer verification and later design work is the subject of @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

![**Nested boundaries turn authorized requests into qualified execution records.** The environment enforces clean separation across tool wrappers, execution harnesses, and outer sandboxes. Isolating tool state, capturing execution costs, and logging environment metadata ensure that returned simulation and synthesis artifacts remain auditable before reaching downstream feedback. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/ch06-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch06-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which nested environment, harness, wrapper, and tool boundaries turn an authorized request into a complete execution record for later qualification."}

## Architecture of the Tool Execution Harness

Consider an automated optimizer evaluating the cache hierarchy candidates introduced in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization when it requests an evaluation of one candidate under a specified memory workload. Once the environment validates the typed request, it maps the parameter vector to simulator configuration files, provisions CPU affinity and memory limits on a compute node, and launches the binary. When the process exits, the harness parses the log files, extracts miss rates and cycle counts, records the consumed core-hours and memory footprint, and returns an execution record so that the optimizer can inspect that structured record and decide what to explore next.

Now consider the failure case in which a twelve-hour full-system simulation terminates prematurely at hour eight due to an out-of-memory kernel kill and a naive automated script immediately relaunches it. Before trusting the subsequent result, the architect must answer hard operational questions: Did the restart reuse an uncorrupted memory checkpoint or launch from cold reset, did it inherit modified host environment variables or dirty scratch files from the failed attempt, and did the accounting subsystem record the lost eight core-hours against the study's compute budget? Because restarting a command in an ad hoc workflow discards that failure context, the later comparison silently mixes a cold start with a resumed run.

An execution environment therefore provides both an external interface for the exploration method and the operational machinery behind that interface: whereas the external interface defines what actions a method can request and what structured feedback returns, the internal machinery orchestrates the processes, isolated filesystems, license tokens, and hardware resources required to carry out those actions safely. While human engineers shoulder this operational burden manually in an interactive computer-aided design (CAD) flow by inspecting logs, cleaning scratch directories, and monitoring license queues, automated loops must handle this orchestration programmatically at scale across many concurrent candidates and heterogeneous tools.[^fn-sandboxing-kubernetes-c06] Separating the components that perform this work lets a team assemble a minimal harness first and scale it as the study grows.

[^fn-sandboxing-kubernetes-c06]: **The orchestration parallel**: A correct tool script does not by itself control the state of concurrent or interrupted runs. Containers and workflow schedulers provide useful mechanisms for software execution, but an architecture environment must also coordinate tool-specific checkpoints, shared CAD licenses, and restricted design inputs. The harness performs this coordination for generated requests as well as requests written by an engineer.


### From Tools to an Execution Environment

An exploration algorithm interacts with the environment through typed requests and structured observations. Inside the boundary, five distinct concepts connect speculative requests to physical or simulated computation:

- **Tool**: The standalone executable that performs a domain-specific transformation or analysis, such as compiling software with LLVM, synthesizing register-transfer level (RTL) code into gates with Yosys, or evaluating physical timing with OpenSTA. It consumes files in proprietary or standard formats and emits log reports or physical artifacts.
- **Simulator**: A specialized class of tool that models hardware or software behavior over time. For example, gem5 executes an event-driven, cycle-level microarchitectural model, yielding cycle counts, cache hit distributions, and bus contention statistics under configured workload assumptions.
- **Wrapper**: The adapter that bridges an individual tool to the environment's typed contract. It validates request parameters, generates tool-specific command scripts and configuration files, manages process invocation, parses unstructured text logs into strongly typed metrics, and flags syntax or runtime anomalies.
- **Harness**: The workflow coordinator that orchestrates multi-tool execution pipelines. It resolves candidate dependency graphs, manages concurrent dispatch, arbitrates shared resources such as license tokens and GPU queues, handles timeouts and retries, and binds execution outcomes to parent artifacts.
- **Environment**: The overarching system that encapsulates the design state, permitted action space, tool interfaces, and security sandboxes. It governs what the search method can observe, modify, and evaluate, establishing the boundary between algorithmic strategy and physical execution.

Suppose a generative model proposes a revised cache coherence controller in RTL and requests behavioral validation. The wrapper synthesizes a custom testbench driver, launches Verilator inside an isolated scratch directory, and extracts assertion outcomes. The harness tracks that run, logs its memory and CPU consumption, and, upon a functional pass, automatically triggers downstream gate-level synthesis through Yosys. The environment dictates whether the generator may modify arbitrary state machines, tune clock periods in a Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) file, or merely sweep buffer capacities within a fixed netlist. Supporting generated microarchitectures therefore means handling new code artifacts and changing dependency graphs, rather than merely sweeping scalar parameters across a static model.

The operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers place different demands on this execution environment (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration).

For Layer 1 work, execution usually remains open-loop. A generative model proposes an isolated code snippet, such as a first-in, first-out (FIFO) buffer or an arbiter, but the environment interaction is manual. The human engineer acts as the execution harness, pasting generated RTL into a local workspace, invoking the compiler or simulator through interactive shell scripts, and inspecting terminal logs to diagnose syntax errors or port mismatches.

For Layer 2 work, the environment must support automated parameter search within a frozen structural container $\Theta$. An optimizer sweeps architectural parameters $\theta$, such as cache capacities, queue depths, or macro floorplan coordinates, and the environment typically relies on simulators and estimators such as gem5, Ramulator 2, and analytical models to evaluate many variations. Because the prescribed template and external interfaces are fixed, these faster evaluations can guide the search when they have been checked against more detailed analysis over the parameter range in use; that calibration is an obligation of the study, not a property the container supplies.

Layer 3 work permits coordinated changes beyond that template, so candidates can fall outside the range where a fast estimator was calibrated. The environment must support physical implementation and signoff for candidates advanced toward physical commitment, while earlier checks can reject others. A public system reporting such an end-to-end run, from a written specification to a timing-closed layout, is examined against the book's evidence standard in @sec-design-conductor-case. For the environment, the point is that such a run needs the whole tool chain, not a single simulator, inside its boundary.

Existing electronic design automation (EDA) frameworks provide useful building blocks: SiliconCompiler connects design data, tool settings, and process design kit (PDK) information through a shared schema and execution flow [@SiliconCompiler], whereas Hammer separates tool-specific steps, technology information, and project configuration through its plugin interfaces [@Hammer]. Although such frameworks supply reusable hardware-flow knowledge, a study must still define which actions its methods can request and how returned results enter the design loop, just as general build and scheduling systems can support execution only provided the surrounding integration preserves the required design and tool information.

### Host and Network Boundaries

An evaluation request runs on a host with finite resources and access to project data. Several requests may share licenses, processors, and storage, while a generated script can affect whatever its process can reach. The environment therefore needs to control both resource sharing and access. Five concerns illustrate what this means for hardware tools; the appropriate mechanisms depend on the tools, deployment, and study restrictions.

1. **Shared licenses.** Commercial EDA tools often require a license checkout managed by servers such as FlexLM[^fn-flexlm-c06] or Sentinel before work can proceed, so launching more compute workers cannot increase throughput once seats are exhausted and an unconstrained loop can starve other engineers on the cluster. The harness therefore tracks each request's license requirements alongside its compute requirements, queues work when capacity is unavailable, and monitors checkout status. While a local token pool can coordinate the harness's own requests, it cannot reserve capacity against external users, and recovery after a worker failure must follow the license server's supported timeout and reclamation policy rather than assuming a terminated process has freed its seat.

2. **Restricted data.** Because a study may permit an external model to propose design changes while requiring foundry models and proprietary design files to remain on approved hosts, the environment must enforce those restrictions for process design kit (PDK) collateral, layout views, transistor-level models, and any derived information covered by the study's disclosure policy. While a proxy can mediate requests between an external model and internal tools, its return interface needs equal attention: replacing absolute delays with "Path A is 12% slower than Path B," or removing die coordinates from a congestion map, reduces detail without establishing that the result may be disclosed, and prompts or abstract syntax tree (AST) edits can also contain proprietary information. The environment therefore needs an explicit definition of what may cross this boundary, including feedback from synthesis, design rule checking (DRC), and layout versus schematic (LVS) checks.

3. **Host runtime variation.** A simulator's elapsed time reflects the machine running it as well as the modeled design, because worker migration across non-uniform memory access (NUMA)[^fn-numa-c06] nodes, competing memory traffic, and central processing unit (CPU) frequency changes all alter execution time and throughput. Where runtime comparisons matter, controlled resource allocation keeps those measurements interpretable: on Linux, CPU affinity tools such as `taskset -c` restrict where threads run while scheduler rules prevent unwanted contention on those cores, CPU frequency policies and storage placement can be pinned, and RAM-backed temporary storage (`/dev/shm` or `tmpfs`) absorbs I/O when its memory footprint fits the allocation. Although these controls reduce host interference, they do not make a nondeterministic tool deterministic; @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion separates host timing variation from changes in returned design results.

4. **Generated scripts and host access.** Because a synthesis script is executable input in which Tcl commands such as `exec` and pipeline forms of `open` can launch programs with the permissions available to the tool process, a generated script can overwrite files or make network requests beyond the intended design operation. To grant execution only the files, permissions, and network access that operation requires, an environment can combine unprivileged Open Container Initiative (OCI) containers, user namespaces, read-only library and PDK mounts, restricted network access, and system-call filters such as seccomp.[^fn-seccomp-c06] Each mechanism addresses a different facet of isolation, so a container alone does not establish the required boundary if exposed mounts and file permissions remain overly broad.

5. **Storage and retained artifacts.** Physical design tools produce large databases, checkpoints, and exchange files, including Synopsys NDM databases, DEF layout data, Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF) parasitics, and GDSII streams,[^fn-physical-checkpoints-c06] so concurrent writes can saturate shared storage and leave otherwise available processors waiting. Although local scratch storage can absorb active writes, the environment must move needed outputs to persistent storage before reclaiming a workspace. Because what must remain depends on subsequent work (where a parser failure may require raw reports, a resumed run needs its checkpoint, and result review may require more than extracted metrics), failed or filtered candidates still need the material required for their recovery and review, whereas large intermediates can be removed once those uses no longer require them so long as the retained record states what remains available.

[^fn-flexlm-c06]: **License checkout**: A tool requests access to a licensed feature before using it. Depending on the tool's integration with the license manager, unavailable capacity may cause the request to wait or fail; the harness must distinguish that outcome from an analysis that ran and found a design problem.

[^fn-numa-c06]: **NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access)**: A computer memory design where memory access time depends on the memory location relative to the processor. Under NUMA, a processor can access its own local memory faster than non-local memory (memory local to another processor or shared between processors).

[^fn-seccomp-c06]: **seccomp (secure computing mode)**: A Linux kernel feature that restricts the system calls a process can make, reducing the exposed kernel surface. It is one component of containment, not a complete sandbox.

[^fn-physical-checkpoints-c06]: **Physical design checkpoints**: During chip layout, tools generate massive intermediate files. DEF (Design Exchange Format) stores the placement and routing of components. SPEF (Standard Parasitic Exchange Format) records the resistance and capacitance of the wires for timing analysis. GDSII is the final binary format representing the 2D shapes of the chip's masks, ultimately sent to the foundry for manufacturing.


### Tool Wrappers

Host and network controls determine where execution can occur and what it can access. A wrapper connects the method's request to the tool running within those limits. Suppose a generator submits revised controller code for synthesis under a specified clock constraint and cell library. If the tool uses a default clock period or a different library, it answers a different question even if it exits successfully. The wrapper must translate the request explicitly and report any mismatch it can detect. If it cannot express a required setting through the tool's interface, it should refuse the request rather than silently substitute another setting.

Before launch, the wrapper checks that the request contains the required fields, resolves artifact identifiers to the intended source files and libraries, verifies that numeric parameters lie within their allowed ranges, and prepares constraints such as the controller's SDC clock definition. Catching detectable input problems before expensive execution saves cluster compute and license tokens, though a request that passes pre-flight validation can still describe a faulty design or encounter a runtime tool failure rather than establishing design correctness.

The return path needs the same care: once execution yields a process exit code alongside log reports and physical artifacts, a dedicated parser extracts typed metrics, units, and operating conditions while retaining the raw logs for auditability. The harness then binds these outputs to the originating request and records consumed compute and license resources, because keeping these steps separate prevents a translation error or an unparseable log from masquerading as a design result (@fig-environment-tool-interface).

![**Tool wrappers separate raw execution state from semantic result interpretation.** The wrapper validates and translates incoming typed requests before invoking backend tools, while the parser extracts structured attributes and retains unclassified residual output. The harness binds runtime outcomes, parse health, compute costs, and lineage into an immutable execution record. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-environment-tool-interface.svg){#fig-environment-tool-interface width="80%" fig-alt="Flow diagram in which an architecture question and workload, action schema, constraints, and metric definitions enter the tool-connected environment as a typed request. The wrapper validates and translates the request before calling the tool. An invalid request goes directly to the harness record. The tool separately produces raw returned material and a runtime outcome that can be failed, partial, or complete. The parser turns retained raw material into structured attributes, unclassified residual output, and a parse status. The harness records request and attempt identity, conditions, runtime outcome, artifacts, parse status, cost, and lineage."}

When an incoming candidate fails pre-flight validation, such as specifying an illegal cache capacity or an unresolvable technology library, the wrapper short-circuits the request directly to the execution record with a refused status, preventing unbudgeted cluster dispatch and preserving license tokens. When execution proceeds, the tool's runtime outcome (failed, partial, or complete) is captured independently from the parser's extraction status, so downstream methods can distinguish a failed simulation from a completed run whose report the parser could not read. For a synthesis request, the wrapper might return a mapped gate-level netlist and static timing slack. Other wrappers extract gem5 miss rates or power estimates derived from switching activity. In every case, an absent metric remains strictly distinguishable from a measured zero. Retaining raw reports alongside unclassified residual output ensures that silent anomalies, such as unconstrained timing paths or missing clock definitions, remain auditable even when a tool exits with code zero.

This is the distinction between parsing a report and deciding what it supports: although a structured return makes tool feedback usable by a method, it does not by itself establish that the evaluation answers the architectural question, so the wrapper checks and reports what its interface can establish while later analysis examines the retained outputs and conditions. Because even an explicit request and a careful parser are insufficient if the tool inherits unintended state from an earlier run, controlling that state is the next part of preserving the request's meaning.

### Stateful Tools and Exact Translation

A tool's starting state is part of its input, even when that state is absent from the request: a physical design session may already contain a netlist, placement, and routing data, or a simulator may resume from a checkpoint, as when OpenROAD saves and reloads its design database [@OpenROADDocs]. If a generator submits revised controller code while execution resumes from an in-memory database built from the previous version, or if a persistent Tcl shell retains stale Design Exchange Format (DEF) geometries, the resulting report describes the old design. Because dirty `tmpfs` scratch volumes retaining stale Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF) extractions or cached timing graphs across multi-corner static timing analysis (STA) runs likewise silently corrupt delay calculations, correctly parsing that report cannot repair the mismatch.

Starting a fresh process in a clean workspace is one way to control inherited state, provided it loads the intended inputs and environment settings. Reusing a session or checkpoint can save work, but the environment must establish what state is being reused and whether it is suitable for the next operation. A reset must restore the required starting state; a deliberate continuation must identify its checkpoint and prior work. Temporary files, in-memory databases, and inherited environment variables all matter when they can affect execution. The aim is to make reuse explicit and checkable, rather than require a new process for every invocation.

The same problem extends across tools because a candidate has several representations. RTL code describes behavior, while synthesis produces a netlist mapped to a cell library. Yosys, for example, can map logic to cells described by a target library [@Yosys]. Physical implementation then needs the matching library information: Liberty (`.lib`) files supply timing and power characterization, while Library Exchange Format (LEF) files describe physical abstractions used during layout. OpenROAD consumes these inputs alongside the design [@OpenROADDocs]. A power-aware flow also needs applicable power intent. Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1801 Unified Power Format (UPF) describes matters such as power domains and isolation requirements; it does not itself estimate power.[^fn-eda-formats-c06]

[^fn-eda-formats-c06]: **EDA formats**: Liberty (`.lib`) files describe cell timing and power, while Library Exchange Format (LEF) files describe physical abstractions such as dimensions, pins, and routing obstructions. Unified Power Format (UPF) supplies power intent, including power domains and isolation strategies; it describes requirements for a power-aware implementation rather than supplying that implementation itself.


All of these files must describe compatible design and operating assumptions, because merely collecting files under the same candidate identifier does not establish that they belong together. If a generator alters a block's interface while leaving an old physical abstraction in place, modifies power domains without updating the UPF power intent, or runs analysis against a library characterized at 0.75\ V when the request specifies another voltage, the returned timing and power describe a mismatched design or operating condition. The environment must therefore track which inputs each tool path depends on and verify their compatibility before admitting its results.

Translating a request into tool-specific syntax introduces a related obligation: a wrapper may convert units or reformat settings, and different tools may legitimately use different abstractions of a candidate when the modeled properties and limitations remain explicit, but silently rounding a capacity or changing an array dimension creates a different candidate. When a backend cannot represent a required feature, the wrapper should return that limitation so the design loop can choose another evaluation path, because changing the candidate to make execution succeed is a new design proposal rather than a translation repair.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Preserve the requested design across every tool boundary"}
**The principle:** A wrapper translates a request into a tool's syntax without changing the candidate, its operating conditions, or its starting state; when it cannot, it refuses the request or reports the limitation.

**The application:** A run that used a default clock, a different library view, a rounded capacity, or state inherited from an earlier attempt still carries the requested candidate's identity while describing a different design. Check translation, starting state, and input compatibility before launch, and give any change made only to get a run through its own identity as a new proposal.
:::

The Lighthouse study shows what that rule demands when one candidate must reach several tools.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One XR SoC request, several tool representations"}
**Context.** The prospective Lighthouse study illustrates how one candidate can require different tool inputs without changing the design under comparison.

**Application.** Consider a candidate with a 3\ MiB cache, a neural processing unit (NPU) array ($16 \times 16$), and dual LPDDR5X channels. An analytical model would use the dimensions and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) assumptions relevant to its estimates. A configured gem5 model would represent the supported timing behavior, while a Verilator-based path would execute the supplied RTL and testbench. Each path would need matching workload inputs or traffic generators and an explicit account of which candidate features it represents.

**Required behavior.** Wrappers must preserve relevant capacities, dimensions, cache policies, and memory arbitration wherever those properties are modeled. An unsupported feature must be reported rather than silently replaced by a default. Differences between tool outputs must be interpreted in light of their models and conditions. These are requirements for the unexecuted study, not observed wrapper results.
:::

## Environment Provisioning, Typed Interfaces, and Tool Lineage

Before an optimization or generation method can use an environment, the harness must establish how it accepts candidate artifacts (such as revised SystemVerilog modules, simulator configurations, or compiler schedules) and how it tracks every tool invocation they trigger. Provisioning defines how design sources, process libraries, and workload inputs are identified, what typed requests each tool wrapper accepts and returns, and which tool paths evaluate behavioral correctness, cycle-level throughput, or physical timing and power.

The candidates themselves need not all exist when the study starts. As a generator proposes new controller RTL or modifies a cache parameter during the loop, the environment registers each new artifact, binds it to the exact library views, constraints, and workload snapshots it requires, and dispatches it to the appropriate tools. Recording those inputs and operating conditions at submission time ensures that every returned report can be traced back to the exact configuration that produced it. The first setup question is therefore how to preserve this lineage as candidate revisions and tool outputs accumulate.

### Lineage and Reproducibility

When a design changes, the dependency graph determines which existing artifacts still apply and which must be regenerated. *Lineage* records the history linking requests, transformations, and artifacts: which inputs produced an output, which candidate an evaluation used, and how a retry relates to an earlier attempt. Setup establishes how these relationships will be recorded as work proceeds. Retained input versions, such as source snapshots, constraints, and library files, remain separate from mutable working files so that later edits do not erase what an earlier run used.

Compilation and hardware elaboration turn source descriptions into representations that downstream tools can consume, including abstract syntax trees, control-data flow graphs (CDFGs), and gate netlists. A lineage entry connects its output to the inputs and settings used to produce it. The useful information includes:

- Parent candidate and request identifiers, including the originating attempt when work is retried.
- Transformation tool and compiler versions, together with the settings used.
- Input and output content hashes, which identify the retained file contents.
- Applicable operating conditions and references to the required libraries or models.
- Checks performed on the transformation, their outcomes, and any properties left unchecked.
- Downstream uses permitted by the study, including any restrictions on the resulting artifacts.

These records form a dependency graph: when a parameter in a high-level C++ hardware model changes, artifacts derived from that parameter, such as generated RTL and its synthesized netlist, must be regenerated or otherwise shown to remain applicable before reuse. While a software testbench can remain unchanged if it does not depend on the changed behavior or interface, it is affected too whenever the same parameter determines its expected outputs, so selective rebuilding works only when the recorded dependencies include the inputs that actually influence each transformation.

Invalidation then walks the transformation history, so that history has to be kept as an explicit directed acyclic graph (@fig-artifact-lineage) in which a later iteration can add branches without rewriting the lineage of earlier evaluations.

![**Evaluated software and hardware artifacts retain explicit parent transformation lineage.** A single architectural intent branches into parallel software compilation and hardware elaboration paths. Each intermediate artifact (binary executable, Verilog RTL, gate netlist) inherits cryptographic parent hashes, tool versions, and operating conditions. Modifying any upstream input or configuration generates a distinct evaluation identity rather than overwriting existing records. The diagram is schematic; its hash labels are placeholders, not recorded digests.](images/fig-artifact-lineage.svg){#fig-artifact-lineage width="80%" fig-alt="Lineage diagram in which a single Lighthouse intent branches into a software variant and a hardware variant. The software compiles into an identified binary, and the hardware elaborates into an identified RTL artifact. An evaluation instance binds both artifacts to the tool and version, workload, and operating conditions. Hashes and evaluation keys distinguish exact artifacts and paths but do not prove functional equivalence or reproducibility."}

To identify the exact combination being evaluated, the environment constructs an evaluation key from all declared inputs that distinguish evaluations, including content hashes of the design artifacts and workload, tool and container versions, and relevant settings. Because recording parent hashes alone cannot uncover a missing dependency, a changed compiler version can produce a new evaluation key even if the output binary is unchanged, whereas repeated executions of the same identified configuration still receive separate execution records so their individual outcomes and costs remain distinct.

Conditions belong in this history as well: for physical timing, a slack of -12\ ps at a slow corner and the same value at a typical corner describe different operating cases, so that although they can be compared with those conditions in view, they cannot be treated as interchangeable observations. Because software measurements also depend on details beyond the source program, where experiments have shown that link order and environment-variable layout can bias performance comparisons [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData], the practical lesson is to retain the execution conditions that can affect the property being measured.

Recording this lineage makes an evaluation traceable and supplies the metadata needed to repeat it, though proving that a transformation preserved behavior or that another execution will reproduce the result still requires the relevant verification checks, accessible artifacts, and a working execution procedure. Likewise, while lineage records can confirm whether a checkpoint belongs to the requested configuration, the tool's resume protocol must establish the intended starting state before tool interfaces carry these identities and dependencies consistently through requests and returns.

### Typed Tool Interfaces

During setup, the environment contract defines the actions a method can take by specifying each action's inputs, permitted changes, preconditions, and returned information. Types make those structural requirements explicit (distinguishing a source-code reference, a clock period with units, and an execution-time limit even when a command-line tool ultimately receives them all as text), while the contract defines what the fields mean and how they relate, since type checking alone cannot establish that a library matches a design or that a requested analysis is appropriate.

For the controller example, an environment might expose separate actions to submit an implementation, synthesize an identified version, and evaluate its timing. A synthesis request would identify the source artifact, top-level module, library, and constraints; its return would identify any generated netlist and reports alongside execution and parsing status. If the study holds the library fixed, the interface should resolve that setting from the study configuration and reject conflicting requests. An interface that accepts a new implementation lets a generator revise the design anywhere within the study's scope, whereas one limited to selecting values for predefined parameters confines it to the changes that parameter list anticipates.

While interfaces across the tool classes in @tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum can share fields for request identifiers, execution status, output references, cost, and error information, and submission and cancellation behavior can follow common conventions, tool-specific inputs and outputs still need their own definitions. Interfaces to synthesis with Yosys and physical implementation with OpenROAD, for example, must accommodate the different artifacts and constraints those operations require [@Yosys; @AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD], because a timing slack and an architectural simulator's instructions per cycle (IPC) estimate cannot become interchangeable simply because both are returned as numeric fields, just as an adapter for a commercial tool has to account for that tool's capabilities, formats, and access restrictions.

When an action changes design structure, a structured intermediate representation (IR) can make the allowed transformation easier to express and check: Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) builds on Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) and provides dialects, or sets of operations and types, for hardware descriptions whose `hw`, `comb`, and `seq` dialects represent module structure, combinational logic, and sequential elements [@CIRCT]. Although an interface can use these structures to identify the operation or module to change instead of relying on text substitution alone, a well-formed representation still requires appropriate behavioral checks after a change because structural validity does not establish that the revised design meets its specification.

Before a method relies on an interface implementation, small fixtures should test it by pairing requests with expected tool inputs and representative reports with expected parsed returns, covering unit conversion, unsupported settings, and missing outputs alongside successful requests. Following the precedent of systematic recovery testing in distributed systems such as FATE and DESTINI [@GunawiEtAl2011FATEDestini], failure injection should also exercise hardware-tool failure modes (including timeouts, terminated processes, and truncated reports) to verify that the interface returns the promised status and retains useful diagnostics. With individual actions and their failure behaviors verified, the next question is which combination of tools can evaluate the properties the study needs.

### Multi-Tool Toolchains and Fidelity

A revised controller raises several questions: does it behave correctly, how does it affect workload execution, and can its implementation meet timing? Different tools address different parts of that evaluation. @sec-data-representations-world-models explains which sources reveal which properties; here the environment binds those sources into executable tool paths. Each path requires its own inputs, model assumptions, and outputs, even when it starts from the same candidate.

Fidelity describes how well a model represents the property under study rather than establishing a universal ranking of tools. Because an RTL simulation can expose behavior that an analytical model omits, a physical timing analysis addresses delays that an unannotated RTL simulation does not model, and a formal check answers a specified correctness question under its assumptions, greater detail in one of these evaluations cannot replace the others.

Because these complementary tool classes answer distinct questions rather than forming a linear sequence that every candidate must traverse (@tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum), a study can stage its work economically, running independent checks in parallel while using fast estimates to screen candidates before more expensive evaluations whenever the screening method is suitable for the property and operating range.

How much of this staging a study needs depends on how much the automated work may change: whereas a search inside a fixed structural template can sometimes rely mainly on one fidelity tier, such as cycle-level simulation or an analytical wirelength proxy, when the template has already been implemented and the explored parameter range stays within the region where that tier was checked, structural changes remove that assurance. Because unconventional proposals can exploit gaps in heuristic estimators and a generated topology can raise instructions per cycle in simulation yet prove unroutable or fail power-integrity checks, an environment for structural search arranges the tool classes of @tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum into staged evaluation, where fast analytical and functional models screen candidates, cycle-level models evaluate dynamic throughput, and physical implementation and signoff tools check the properties the faster models omit within the limits of their own libraries, corners, and assumptions.

| **Tool class** | **Representative use** | **What it models or checks** | **Preserved environment state** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical / circuit model | CACTI, spreadsheet models [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI]. | Analytical equations and technology assumptions without workload execution. | Model version, macro geometry, PVT conditions, technology limits. |
| Compiler and build stack | TVM, IREE, LLVM pass pipelines, linkers. | Generation of executable binaries; no hardware timing. | Source intermediate representations (IRs), target instruction set architecture (ISA) flags, compiler versions, binary hashes. |
| Functional ISA emulator | Spike, QEMU ISA execution. | Instruction semantics without microarchitectural timing. | Target binary, ISA extensions, input state, functional output. |
| Timing simulation | gem5 [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5], SST, Ramulator 2, SCALE-Sim. | Pipeline, cache, network-on-chip (NoC), memory controller, and accelerator timing. | Workload inputs, traces, warmup length, seeds, event traces. |
| RTL simulation / testbench | Verilator [@Veripool2026Verilator], cocotb, Synopsys VCS. | Cycle behavior under RTL semantics; no routed delay unless annotated. | RTL hash, testbench, compile flags, waveform traces. |
| Formal verification | SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and bounded model checking (BMC) via SymbiYosys or JasperGold [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. | Stated invariants/relations under declared proof methods and bounds. | Property definitions, bounds, solver engine, proof certificates. |
| Emulation and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) | ZeBu, Palladium, FireSim on cloud FPGAs [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. | Accelerated target execution. FPGA mapping is not application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) signoff. | Target bitstream, host allocation, workload snapshot, traces. |
| Physical implementation and signoff | OpenROAD flow; OpenSTA timing; KLayout / Calibre DRC/LVS [@OpenROADDocs]. | Placement, routing, extracted parasitics, timing closure, and physical design-rule checks. | Netlist, library/PDK views, SDC constraints, layout and parasitic artifacts, operating corners, stage settings, rule decks. |
: **Fidelity is relative to the property under evaluation.** Harnesses preserve model assumptions, inputs, stages, and artifacts rather than collapsing returns into scalar scores. {#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[20,24,28,28]"}

The meaning of a return depends on how the tool was used. A formal result must identify the property and assumptions, and distinguish bounded checking from an inductive proof such as $k$-induction.[^fn-k-induction-c06] A completed bounded check does not establish behavior beyond its bound. This information belongs with the result so that the next method can use it within its scope.

[^fn-k-induction-c06]: **$k$-induction**: A formal proof method with two obligations. The base case establishes the property along executions from allowed initial states through the chosen depth. The inductive step establishes that, for any transition sequence admitted by the model, the property holding for $k$ consecutive states implies that it holds in the next state. Both obligations must succeed under the declared assumptions to establish the invariant beyond a bounded check.

Sampling introduces another kind of qualification. SimPoint and SMARTS[^fn-simpoint-smarts-c06] let simulators evaluate selected intervals and estimate the full workload's behavior [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The environment must retain the interval-selection method, applicable weights, warmup choices, and any checkpoint dependencies. These identify what execution was sampled and how its observations contribute to the estimate.

[^fn-simpoint-smarts-c06]: **Simulation sampling**: SimPoint selects intervals based on program phases; SMARTS uses systematic sampling. Both reduce the amount of detailed execution that must be simulated. Their sampling and warmup assumptions remain part of the resulting performance estimate.


A unified design configuration connects these disparate evaluation paths across a project. In an SoC integration framework such as Chipyard [@chipyard], a single root configuration lowers through Chisel elaboration and FIRRTL transformations before fanning out into specialized evaluation backends (@fig-chipyard-framework). This shared origin lets software RTL simulation, physical VLSI implementation, and FPGA-accelerated execution start from the same microarchitectural parameters. Branch-specific settings and transformations must still be recorded independently; a shared top-level configuration guarantees common starting parameters, but it does not ensure that different backends evaluate identical physical or timing behavior.

![**Unified design configurations anchor multi-tool evaluation flows.** In this architectural flow based on the Chipyard SoC framework [@chipyard], a single root configuration lowers through Chisel generation and FIRRTL transformations before fanning out into specialized evaluation toolchains: software RTL simulation (Verilator/Synopsys VCS), very-large-scale integration (VLSI) physical design (Hammer with OpenROAD or commercial engines), and FPGA-accelerated simulation (FireSim). Shared configuration lineage preserves parameter traceability across fidelity tiers without conflating distinct physical returns. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-chipyard-framework.svg){#fig-chipyard-framework width="80%" fig-alt="Flow diagram in which a common design configuration lowers through Chisel generation and compiler transformations before branching into RTL simulation, VLSI physical implementation, and FPGA-accelerated simulation."}

Although shared configuration history traces a result back to its originating candidate, each output retains the semantic limitations of its specific evaluation path: cycle counts from an unannotated Verilator testbench cannot substitute for post-route timing slack, FPGA execution rates are not ASIC clock frequencies, and FPGA resource utilization may reward a design that maps efficiently to lookup tables without establishing its standard-cell area. Because using such a quantity as a predictor requires evidence for that relationship, the environment must retain the tool, model, conditions, and units with each metric so that the method can distinguish these uses.

Throughput also depends on the configuration being evaluated: while ZSim reports about 20\ MIPS (million instructions per second) per simulated core with about $200\times$ slowdown for its detailed out-of-order model [@ZSim], the FireSim paper reports a 1,024-node target cluster running at a simulated processor clock rate of 3.4\ MHz, less than $1{,}000\times$ slower than its 3.2\ GHz target [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Because instructions per second and target cycles per second count different work while the reported slowdown factors depend on their respective reference systems, these figures describe different modeled systems rather than a direct performance comparison.

@tbl-ch06-simulation-spectrum pairs each execution path with a reporting unit and the conditions that comparisons must match. After selecting a tool that observes the required property, the environment can budget its work in those units. Preparing a compiled simulator or FPGA image also consumes time, so the execution plan must distinguish preparation cost from the cost of subsequent runs that reuse it.

| **Execution path** | **Unit of work or elapsed time** | **Conditions to match** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Analytical model | Model evaluations / second | Model, candidate size, host |
| ISA execution | Instructions / second | ISA, workload, host |
| Timing / RTL simulation | Target cycles / host second | Target model, workload, host |
| Hardware emulation | Target cycles / host second | Mapped target, workload, testbed |
| Formal verification | Elapsed time / named property | Property, model, bound, solver |
| Physical implementation | Elapsed time / defined stage | Design, libraries, stage settings |
: **Throughput comparisons require a declared unit of work.** Different execution paths count different work: model evaluations, instructions, target cycles, properties, or physical flow stages. The final column identifies conditions needed before even two rates in the same row can be compared. Row order implies no throughput or fidelity ranking. Author-constructed comparison guide, not a measured benchmark. {#tbl-ch06-simulation-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[28,34,38]"}

Frameworks provide different parts of this integration. ArchGym connects search algorithms to architecture simulators [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym], while CHIA supports hardware-software co-design workflows that combine design tools, simulators, software builds, and model calls [@CuiEtAl2026CHIA]. Workflow engines such as Nextflow and Snakemake can manage execution dependencies [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow; @KosterEtAl2012Snakemake]. The study still has to specify which tool path answers each question, which artifacts pass between stages, and what conditions permit reuse. Once those paths are configured, the harness must manage their execution as requests queue, run, and return.

## Runtime Orchestration, Fault Isolation, and Execution State

Once the tool paths are configured, the runtime harness manages how jobs actually execute on cluster nodes. It admits requests as compute slots and EDA licenses become available, tracks active simulations and synthesis runs, and returns parsed reports alongside exit status and resource costs. Because tools write intermediate databases, scratch directories, and checkpoints as they run, the harness must isolate each attempt's working state and keep it bound to the exact inputs and checkpoints it used.

An active search loop often proposes a new candidate while an earlier multi-hour gem5 simulation or OpenROAD place-and-route job is still running. The new submission must not overwrite RTL or constraint files in a live workspace, and a cluster preemption must not erase the accounting record of work already performed. An asynchronous interface lets the optimizer submit a candidate and continue exploring while the harness tracks in-flight attempts, isolates failures, and determines when completed artifacts can be reused. The first runtime requirement is therefore submitting and monitoring jobs without accidentally launching duplicate runs.

### Asynchronous Scheduling and Idempotency

A synchronous interface returns the result of an action through the call that requested it. The `step()` interface in reinforcement learning (RL) environments such as Gymnasium follows this pattern [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium]. It is convenient when evaluations finish quickly. For long-running architecture work, separating submission from completion lets a method monitor outstanding requests and continue other work while tools execute. A scheduler adapter connects the harness to an execution backend, such as Slurm, IBM LSF, or a container service.

The harness must distinguish what was requested from how it executes: whereas a request describes the intended evaluation and an attempt records one effort to carry it out, backend jobs perform that work across compute nodes. Because one attempt can map to zero, one, or many backend jobs, the harness keeps its durable execution record separate from those transient jobs (@fig-runtime-object-state), so that a refused request retains an execution record without ever launching a cluster job while an admitted request may launch a single process or fan out across multiple parallel execution segments whose outputs, exit causes, and compute costs are reconciled into that single record. When a run fails and policy permits a retry, the harness creates a new attempt linked explicitly to its predecessor.

![**A single execution record tracks zero, one, or multiple backend tool executions.** The execution record anchors all backend tool executions to the authorized request, whether the request is refused prior to execution, creates a single tool job, or spawns multiple parallel execution segments. The record preserves returned raw artifacts, realized compute and license costs, and independent status attributes including scheduling state, terminal cause, parser health, and retry parent links. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-runtime-object-state.svg){#fig-runtime-object-state width="80%" fig-alt="Conceptual state diagram in which an authorized request creates one attempt. The attempt may be refused before a backend job exists, may create one job, or may create several jobs or execution segments. All paths feed one execution record. The execution record points separately to returned artifacts and realized cost. Scheduling state, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, cancellation confirmation, and retry parent remain independent attributes."}

Because an execution record must survive the processes that perform its work, the harness retains available logs and records the resources already consumed whenever a cluster scheduler preempts a simulation. Keeping its six independent status attributes (scheduling state, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser health, cancellation confirmation, and retry parentage) separate stops one status from standing in for another: whereas a scheduler may requeue an evicted job under the same attempt so that each execution segment remains part of its cumulative cost history, a harness that instead launches a fresh recovery attempt records a new execution record linked to its predecessor, ensuring that neither path erases the interruption or the consumed core-hours.

Now suppose the harness accepts a submission, but its reply never reaches the caller. Sending the request again must not launch another copy of the work. An *idempotent* submission produces the same system state when repeated. When a caller resubmits the same `submission_token`, the harness returns the existing attempt rather than creating another [@Featonby2021IdempotentAPIs]. Reusing that token with changed request contents should be rejected. A deliberate retry of failed work uses a new token and creates a linked attempt; it is different from retransmitting a submission whose outcome is unknown.

Because providing this behavior requires more than attaching a token, the harness records the accepted attempt before dispatch and retains its association with the token, request, and backend jobs, so that if it crashes during dispatch, recovery must determine whether work already exists before launching it again. Until that state is established, `poll` returns `RECONCILING` to indicate that the attempt is known while its execution state remains uncertain; the caller can continue polling rather than submitting the same work under a new token that could create a duplicate, and recovery must resolve the uncertainty rather than treating it as evidence that no job started.

The interface in @lst-harness-interface separates these operations. `submit` returns an attempt identifier and admission status; `poll` reports progress; `collect` retrieves the execution record once the attempt reaches a terminal state, including any partial outputs and failures. When several jobs belong to an attempt, the harness must define how their states determine the attempt's status. One completed job cannot by itself establish that the whole attempt is complete. `cancel` requests termination, which must be confirmed for all attached work.

To track execution across distributed nodes, the harness needs an explicit state machine for backend jobs (@fig-job-lifecycle). Cluster schedulers preempt long-running simulations and reclaim compute nodes, and the harness has to handle those intermediate transitions without corrupting the attempt they belong to.

![**Explicit scheduling states isolate cluster preemption from candidate evaluation.** A backend job transitions from queued through running to terminal completed, failed, or evicted states. Preempted runs requeue without losing prior execution segments, while retries generate linked attempts. Terminal states finalize compute and license accounting without conflating process termination with architectural validity. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-job-lifecycle.svg){#fig-job-lifecycle width="85%" fig-alt="State machine diagram in which an admitted job transitions from queued to running, branching into terminal completed or failed states, or an evicted state that cycles back to queued."}

A transition to `Completed` indicates only that the underlying operating system process exited with code zero; it does not guarantee that the tool generated valid metrics or satisfied design constraints. In a static timing engine, a clean exit can occur even when unconstrained clock paths mask real violations or when false-path waivers suppress critical timing endpoints. Conversely, an `Evicted` state reflects external scheduler preemption or node reclamation rather than candidate invalidity, requiring automated requeueing while preserving lineage across multiple execution segments. Exploration methods see only the attempt states that @lst-harness-interface returns, not the backend churn beneath them.

```{.yaml #lst-harness-interface lst-cap="**Harness interface shape.** Three normal-path calls submit, poll, and collect an attempt. Polling distinguishes unresolved execution state from known progress or completion. A fourth operation requests cancellation and reports whether termination is confirmed. Refused requests also retain an identifier and a collectable record."}
submit:
  takes: typed request, submission_token
  returns: attempt_id, admission status (ADMITTED | REFUSED)
poll:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: >-
    REFUSED | QUEUED | RUNNING | EVICTED | RECONCILING |
    COMPLETED | FAILED | CANCELED
collect:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: execution record (artifacts, parse status, cost, lineage)
cancel:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: CONFIRMED after all attached work stops | UNCONFIRMED (quarantine)
```

Idempotency prevents duplicate work, but it does not limit the number of distinct requests. The capacity analysis in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization explains why a fast proposal method can overload a slower evaluation stage. The runtime responsibility is to enforce that capacity plan through admission limits, bounded queues, and backpressure, which asks the caller to slow or pause submissions. Capacity at one stage does not imply capacity at the next; available processors may still be waiting for licenses or dependent results.

The same limit applies to licenses, and there it has a second failure. License managers grant checkouts per licensed feature, such as compilation, simulation runtime, or waveform viewing, rather than as interchangeable slots. Suppose an upstream job holds a compilation license while it waits for a simulation license, and the job holding that simulation license waits in turn for a compilation license. Both jobs now hold one resource while waiting for another in a cycle, which meets the conditions for deadlock [@CoffmanEtAl1971SystemDeadlocks]. Reserving every license a job will need before admitting it removes the hold-and-wait condition, and queue limits keep the backlog below the stage capacities. Neither guarantees that a result returns before its input assumptions have moved when tool durations or upstream changes are unpredictable (@sec-law-congestion-collapse in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).

### Fault Containment and Execution Quarantines

Suppose a synthesis run reaches its time limit and the harness requests cancellation: if the launcher exits while a worker it started is still writing a design database, reusing that workspace for a retry could mix files from two attempts. Fault containment limits the effect of this unfinished work on other executions because it requires control of the processes and writable resources belonging to an attempt, together with a way to determine whether they are still active.

On Linux, control groups (cgroups) can track a job's local processes together. The cgroup v2 `cgroup.kill` interface targets processes in a group and its descendants, while the group's status can indicate whether live processes remain.[^fn-process-containment-c06] Packaging commercial EDA flows into rootless OCI containers adds further isolation, but requires addressing specific enterprise constraints: license checkout can depend on host network access or on host identifiers such as a network-interface hardware address; shared high-throughput scratch filesystems require POSIX file locking across network mounts; and multi-threaded signoff engines require tuned shared-memory (`/dev/shm`) allocations. The harness must arrange for the relevant workers to belong to the tracked groups and confirm that attached work has stopped before reclaiming its resources. Remote workers require corresponding control through their execution backend; terminating the local launcher does not establish that remote work has ended.

[^fn-process-containment-c06]: **Process containment**: Commercial EDA tools can spawn background daemons and child processes. If a parent script is killed, live orphaned workers may continue consuming memory and holding licenses. They differ from zombie processes, which have exited and await reaping. Linux `cgroups` (control groups) keep a job's processes in a tracked group so the harness can terminate them together and confirm exit before reclaiming resources.


If process termination cannot be confirmed, the harness quarantines the affected execution by isolating the workspace, withholding partial outputs from publication, and marking uncertain allocations as unavailable for new work as an enforced restriction on reuse rather than merely a status label. Although a late write may still reach the old workspace, it must not reach a retry's workspace or shared candidate artifacts, so a retry can use a separate workspace and allocation when those boundaries and the remaining budget permit it while the quarantined attempt remains tracked until the harness resolves its execution state and can safely reclaim the affected resources.

Bounding how much work an attempt can consume requires enforcement mechanisms suited to each resource (model calls, tool submissions, compute time, memory, storage, and licenses), because a process limit does not establish license availability and a submission limit does not bound a running tool's memory use. For commercial tokens, the harness must retain an unresolved allocation until the license server's supported release mechanism establishes that the checkout is available again, rather than inferring release from a cancellation request.

Recovery also has to preserve the study's accounting: a retry of the same design under the same tool settings retains its `candidate_id` and `configuration_id` while receiving a new execution record, whereas any changed inputs or settings must be identified explicitly. Each attempt retains its outputs, measured resource use, and associated costs (including compute time, memory and storage use, license occupancy, and any budgeted human repair effort), recording costs that cannot yet be determined as unknown rather than zero so the method can distinguish unfinished execution from a completed evaluation before deciding how to recover.

### Categorizing Tool and Environment Failures

A stopped or unsuccessful evaluation does not necessarily mean that the candidate is a poor design. A FlexLM[^fn-flexlm-c06] license checkout denial means the tool could not acquire the requested license; a host out-of-memory failure means execution could not obtain the memory it needed. Neither establishes that the hardware is unroutable. If the environment records either event as a design failure, a predictor may learn the wrong label and an optimizer may discard a candidate that has not received the intended evaluation.

Recovery begins by separating what happened during execution from what the returned material says about the design. @tbl-failure-taxonomy lists nine conditions worth retaining. They can overlap: an infrastructure interruption may leave an incomplete report that also causes parsing to fail, while a completed timing analysis may report a constraint violation. Earlier successful evaluations of the candidate remain part of its history even when another attempt fails.

| **Recorded condition** | **How it appears** | **Preserved evidence** | **Runtime response** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Invalid request** | Illegal parameter or meaning-altering translation detected prior to invocation. | Request, validation rule, refusal reason. | Repair syntax only if meaning is preserved; otherwise refuse and return to caller. |
| **Setup / dependency failure** | Missing top-level, clock, library, constraint, or checkpoint. | Setup check, diagnostics, partial artifacts, cost. | Restore or regenerate required inputs; record which evaluation could not proceed. |
| **Infrastructure failure** | License server unreachable, host out-of-memory (OOM), scheduler preemption. | Execution record, failure source, cost, retry eligibility. | Retry if policy and resources permit; retain any partial observations and mark the interrupted evaluation incomplete. |
| **Tool failure** | Crash or tool-reported execution error, such as a gem5 crash or failed elaboration. | Tool diagnostics, exit code, partial artifacts, cost. | Inspect the diagnostic to distinguish tool malfunction, input problems, and reported design errors before choosing recovery. |
| **Incomplete return** | Missing or truncated report files. | Stage records, produced files, raw logs, parse status. | Recover retained files or regenerate missing outputs where possible; rerun only the required work. |
| **Parser failure** | An available report cannot be interpreted according to the expected schema; absent source data may also indicate an incomplete return. | Parser version, raw log, recognized tokens, residual output. | Check the report and parser version; repair parsing and reparse if the required source data is present. |
| **Formal-tool return** | SVA/BMC tool returns a proof, counterexample, bounded result, or unresolved outcome. | Original status, method, property, model, assumptions, bound, available proof or counterexample trace, cost. | Preserve the exact status and its scope, including any timeout or other reason the check remains unresolved. |
| **Reported limit violation** | Completed run reports physical violation (OpenROAD worst negative slack (WNS) $< 0$, DRC error). | Typed violation, units, conditions, raw report, cost. | Record complete return without marking run as tool failure. |
| **Complete tool return** | Expected artifacts exist and parse cleanly (including limit violations). | Typed metrics, units, conditions, warnings, raw logs, cost, lineage. | Retain return for measurement qualification. |
: **Execution status determines what ran, not what the architecture means.** Operational failures, partial returns, parser errors, and physical violations remain separate so recovery targets exact causes. {#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[20,24,28,28]"}

The distinction changes the next action. If a timing tool completed but a parser stopped recognizing its report format, reparsing the retained report may recover the result without another timing run. If the required library was missing, the inputs must be repaired before execution can answer the question. If a completed analysis reports negative slack, repeating the same run is not a remedy for that violation; the design, constraints, or interpretation need examination.

Formal results need similar care. A counterexample identifies a violation of the stated property in the supplied model, while a solver timeout leaves the question unresolved. A proof applies under its recorded assumptions, and bounded checking has a specified scope [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. The harness should retain the tool's original status and supporting material alongside any normalized fields, so that a common interface does not erase these distinctions.

A clean report also has limits because timing and physical checks depend on the tool version, libraries, operating corners, and applied exceptions: if an optimizer adds a false-path exception[^fn-false-path-c06] merely to suppress a timing violation, it has changed what is checked, just as a timing analysis that omits dynamic IR drop[^fn-ir-drop-c06] cannot establish timing under that effect. The environment must therefore retain these settings and analysis assumptions with the result so that raw reports, warnings, and unrecognized log lines remain available when later review discovers that a parsed summary omitted something consequential.

[^fn-false-path-c06]: **False-path waivers**: Timing exceptions that exclude specified paths from static timing checks when functional behavior or clock relationships justify doing so. The exception must be supported by the declared design and clock assumptions; a path's absence from simulation is not sufficient. Asynchronous clock-domain crossings still require appropriate synchronization and clock-domain-crossing checks.

[^fn-ir-drop-c06]: **IR drop**: The voltage reduction (V = I $\times$ R) that occurs as current travels through the resistive metal layers of the power delivery network, which can cause transistors to switch slower or fail entirely under heavy toggle activity.


### Caching and Artifact Reuse

Retained work can reduce the cost of the next evaluation. A compiled simulator may serve several candidates, a generated netlist may feed more than one analysis, and a complete raw report may be reparsed after a parser repair. Each case reuses a different artifact with different dependencies. The runtime question is whether that artifact still applies to the requested operation, not simply whether a file with the expected name exists.

A cache key identifies the inputs and settings used to produce an artifact, where relevant dependencies may include source contents, tool versions, PDK views, flags, workloads, and operating conditions, following the precedent of identifying build outputs through their dependencies in the purely functional deployment model [@Dolstra2006Purely]. Because an omitted library corner or tool default in a hardware flow can still make two apparently matching requests evaluate different conditions, a key is useful only to the extent that its dependencies describe the work being reused, and a matching hash does not establish that a library is appropriate for the requested analysis.

Artifact reuse must also remain visible in the study's accounting, since returning a cached timing report supplies an existing observation rather than an independent repeated measurement; the execution record should therefore point to the producing attempt and distinguish the cost of retrieving the result from the original execution cost. For a generative step, retained model context is a tracked input too, and its reuse must follow the study's data-access and disclosure rules so that context from a proprietary design never silently enters an open-source baseline run.

Whereas retrieving a completed artifact returns an existing output, resuming a checkpoint continues execution from an intermediate state, requiring the harness to identify the checkpoint's inputs, tool configuration, and execution history and establish that it is suitable for the intended continuation. A *reset*, by contrast, restores the starting state required by the next attempt by initializing a fresh workspace or restoring a suitable baseline checkpoint so that tool databases, emulator memory, and other relevant mutable state match that starting state; a soft reset that leaves memory buffers or peripheral registers unchanged is sufficient only if the study permits that retained state and records it.

Stopping a process does not itself perform a reset, and matching checkpoint hashes does not establish that restoration succeeded. License release is a separate resource-management operation, governed by the license server rather than regenerated from design inputs. When work runs again, the record identifies whether it started fresh or continued from retained state and preserves the cost of each execution segment without counting the same work twice. The stale-library example illustrates why this distinction between identity and suitability matters even for a seemingly simple cache hit.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The stale library view"}
**The trap.** In this illustrative failure, a design update reruns static timing analysis and receives a clean report indicating that the checked bus paths meet the requested clock period.

**The mechanism.** The analyzer loaded a cached library view that did not match the intended operating conditions. The report described checks under that stale view; it did not establish timing at the requested conditions.

**The lesson.** Before reusing a library view, the harness must check that it is the view required for the requested design and operating conditions. Checksums help identify PDK, LEF, and Liberty files, but compatibility also depends on their contents and intended use. A clean report from the wrong view cannot establish that the design meets timing under the intended conditions.
:::

### Design Drift and Execution Variability {#sec-incremental-churn-dispersion}

An evaluation may be reproducible for its recorded inputs while no longer answering the team's current design question. During a search against a fixed revision, other work may change compiler passes, runtime software, tool versions, or RTL interfaces. A candidate developed against snapshot $t_0$ may therefore need adaptation and reevaluation before it can be used at $t_0 + \Delta t$. The earlier result still describes its original configuration; it does not automatically transfer to the new one.

The practical question is how much work must be repeated after a change: because regenerating an entire accelerator and repeating physical synthesis for every register or arbiter change can make a search too slow for daily engineering work, a harness can use structural information (such as CIRCT representations, Chisel module hierarchies, and dependency-graph build systems such as Bazel) to identify artifacts affected under its declared dependencies, although reusing other artifacts depends on those dependencies being complete since a file or module boundary on its own cannot establish that a simulation result or formal conclusion remains valid.

Physical implementation makes that limitation concrete. In flattened placement and routing, a local register change can alter congestion, clock-tree structure, and routing elsewhere. Hierarchical partitioning may limit the work to repeat when its interface, timing, and physical assumptions still hold. The harness records the basis for reuse and the work repeated when upstream changes invalidate assumptions. It also tracks changes between an active search snapshot and the mainline, so the study can stop, resynchronize, or repeat affected work under a declared policy.

Revision changes are distinct from variation across repeated executions of the same configuration. To interpret that variation, the environment must keep three mechanisms separate:

- **Host runtime jitter.** CPU frequency changes, NUMA migration, memory contention, and storage contention can change elapsed time and tool throughput without changing the simulated guest cycle count of a deterministic run. Records preserve the host placement, governor, storage path, and other declared runtime conditions.
- **Explicit algorithmic randomness.** Generative methods, stochastic search passes, and randomized EDA stages can produce different candidates, layouts, or metrics. Records preserve seeds where the implementation exposes them, along with sampling and algorithm settings. Unavailable randomness controls must be recorded as a limitation.
- **Parallel execution nondeterminism.** Some tools can return different artifacts or metrics when thread counts or execution schedules change. Records preserve thread and concurrency settings rather than assuming that pinning removes this source of variation.

```{python}
#| echo: false

# Guard for the recipe and seed spreads quoted below: every value is recomputed
# from the chapter dataset and from the retained OpenROAD placement pilot.
import csv
import statistics
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
_recipe_csv = (
    _root / "book" / "contents" / "chapters" / "06-environments" / "data"
    / "fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion.csv"
)
with open(_recipe_csv, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _recipe_rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")))
_areas = {}
for _row in _recipe_rows:
    _areas.setdefault(_row["DesignName"], []).append(float(_row["ChipArea_um2"]))
assert len(_recipe_rows) == 125 and len(_areas) == 5
def _spread_pct(values):
    med = statistics.median(values)
    return 100 * (max(values) - min(values)) / med, med
_router_spread, _ = _spread_pct(_areas["dynamic_node"])
_gcd_spread, _gcd_median = _spread_pct(_areas["gcd"])
assert round(_router_spread, 1) == 3.5 and round(_gcd_spread) == 15
assert round(100 * (min(_areas["gcd"]) / _gcd_median - 1)) == -5
assert round(100 * (max(_areas["gcd"]) / _gcd_median - 1)) == 10

_pilot_csv = (
    _root / "data" / "studies" / "06-eda-seed-dispersion"
    / "openroad_gcd_placement_seed_pilot.csv"
)
with open(_pilot_csv, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _pilot = list(csv.DictReader(fh))
assert len(_pilot) == 20 and all(r["status"] == "pass" for r in _pilot)
_pilot_area = [float(r["detailedplace_instance_area_um2"]) for r in _pilot]
_pilot_wns = [float(r["detailedplace_setup_wns_ns"]) for r in _pilot]
assert round(_spread_pct(_pilot_area)[0], 2) == 0.84
_wns_med = abs(statistics.median(_pilot_wns))
assert round(100 * (max(_pilot_wns) - min(_pilot_wns)) / _wns_med, 1) == 3.8
```

Tool settings that the architecture question does not mention can move returned metrics by amounts comparable to the design differences a study hopes to detect: in one retained dataset of 125 Yosys and ABC logic-synthesis runs targeting the Nangate 45\ nm library, where each of five open designs was mapped under 25 different ABC pass sequences with its RTL unchanged (@fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion), the spread of mapped area ranged from about 3.5% of the median for an OpenPiton NoC router to about 15% for the GCD example block, which computes a greatest common divisor and whose recipes landed between 5% below and 10% above its median. Because every run used a different pass sequence, these spreads measure sensitivity to the recipe rather than run-to-run variation at a fixed recipe, and although the original harness was not retained, a reconstructed flow run on pinned public sources re-derives every recorded area exactly.
