Explicit randomness has its own signature: in a separate pilot with pinned input sources and retained logs, twenty OpenROAD global-placement runs of the GCD example design from OpenROAD-flow-scripts on Nangate45 recorded the same starting floorplan hash and differed only in the placement seed, where the released records include database hashes without the floorplan or placement databases themselves. While detailed-placement area stayed within a 0.84% span of its median and estimated setup WNS spanned 3.8% of its median magnitude across that single small design, flow stage, and host, both results make the same practical point because an optimizer that keeps only favorable outcomes without recording recipes and seeds leaves downstream analysis unable to distinguish an architectural improvement from a tool-setting or seed effect.[^fn-lucky-seed-c06]

[^fn-lucky-seed-c06]: **Seed and recipe sensitivity**: Randomized stages such as stochastic placement, and heuristic settings such as logic-optimization pass order, give a distribution of outcomes rather than a single value. An improvement no larger than the spread across seeds or recipes cannot be attributed to a new method or design without evaluating several seeds or recipes and reporting the spread.

![**Unchanged RTL can return a different mapped area under a different synthesis recipe.** Each point is one of 25 ABC pass sequences applied to one of five open designs with Yosys on the Nangate 45\ nm library, 125 runs in all, plotted relative to each design's median area. The widest spread is on GCD. The runs vary the recipe rather than a random seed, and every plotted area is re-derived by a reconstructed flow on pinned sources.](images/fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion.png){#fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion width="100%" fig-alt="Box plot with overlaid points of 125 logic synthesis runs across five open hardware designs, showing mapped area as a percentage deviation from each design median. Spreads are 3.5 to 7.6 percent for the PicoRV32 core, NoC router, AES-128, and SHA-256 designs and about 15 percent for the GCD block, and each design is drawn with its own marker shape."}

These distributions show why an automated design loop cannot treat a single tool run as a point truth: because heuristic logic-optimization passes such as rewriting, refactoring, and balancing are applied in sequence so that a different sequence can lead the optimization to a different local result with different area, while runtime and memory also depend on the work each sequence performs and on host conditions, a record needs those conditions alongside the result. The study therefore needs to budget for repeated evaluations, record the exact recipes, seeds, and settings, and retain resource consumption alongside quality-of-results metrics, since @sec-feedback-verification-trust explains how downstream statistical methods determine whether an observed gain reflects a genuine architectural improvement or tool variation and the environment's responsibility is to capture the complete execution records that make that evaluation possible.

## Execution Records {#sec-execution-records}

The execution record brings together the information needed to answer three questions: what work was attempted, what happened, and what can be examined afterward? @sec-architecture-20-ontology defines the execution record as the core artifact connecting requested work to the state actually evaluated; here that definition becomes an explicit runtime schema that gathers the identities, outputs, and costs traced through the execution lifecycle. A refused request needs a record even though no tool ran; an attempt with several backend jobs needs their outcomes linked together. A later successful retry adds to this history rather than replacing it.

Six groups of information make the record useful:

- **Request and attempt identity**: Study, request, run specification, candidate, configuration, workload, attempt universally unique identifier (UUID), submission token, and attached scheduler job identifiers.
- **Starting state**: Input artifacts, source revisions, tool and container versions, library views, and operating conditions.
- **Execution outcome**: Admission status, job outcomes, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, and recovery eligibility.
- **Returned material**: Raw reports and logs, artifact references and hashes, structured metrics with units and scope, warnings, and unrecognized output.
- **Lineage and retries**: Dependencies, producing transformations, and links to earlier attempts or restored checkpoints, with references to any checks performed.
- **Resource use and cost**: Wall-clock time, CPU/accelerator hours, peak memory, storage use, license-hours, and charges, distinguishing measured values from estimates or unknowns.

When an expected measurement or artifact is unavailable, the record should state that absence and its cause, if known. This lets later analysis distinguish a quantity that was not measured from one that could not be parsed or did not apply; none should silently become a zero.

Joining inputs, execution status, signoff metrics, and resource costs into one record lets later analysis see what a status or a single summary scalar hides: in static timing analysis, for example, evaluating timing health requires reporting both worst negative slack (WNS, identifying the single most critical path) and total negative slack (TNS, integrating the delay deficit across all failing endpoints) alongside failing endpoint counts and hold slack, because an automated optimizer that evaluates WNS alone can trade away hold-time margin or hide violations spread across many endpoints. While retaining explicit references to raw reports and multi-mode multi-corner (MCMM) views allows independent reviewers to audit which operating paths produced each metric, recording activity profiles, power scopes, and execution costs (wall-clock time, memory footprint, and tool license-hours) likewise lets candidate comparisons weigh the full cost of exploration alongside physical performance.

The depth of record a study needs grows with what the automated work may change: whereas manually driven drafting often keeps informal records such as developer notes, terminal logs, and version-control commits, and a harness running parameter sweeps can automate tracking of parameter vectors, simulator seeds, and scalar cost metrics, a system that changes structure across abstraction boundaries needs records that preserve the chain linking high-level intent, intermediate compiler representations, synthesized netlists, place-and-route databases, and signoff reports, even though such a record documents which checks ran and what they returned rather than certifying on its own that a design is physically viable.


Records also support later attempts to reproduce the work. ACM artifact review guidelines distinguish *repeatability* (same team, same setup), *reproducibility* (different team, same setup), and *replicability* (different team, different setup) [@ACM2020ArtifactReview]. A record supplies information for these activities, but carrying them out also requires access to the artifacts and an executable procedure. The Popper convention similarly emphasizes preserving executable evaluation workflows [@JimenezEtAl2017PopperConvention].

Even with the same recorded inputs, host time or returned results may vary for the reasons discussed in @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion. Lineage identifies how artifacts were produced; references to behavioral checks show what was tested, not what hashes alone prove. The record makes these distinctions available to later analysis. Applying them to a prospective study shows how the environment's rules and its execution history fit together.

## Mobile XR Subsystem Evaluation Environment {#sec-mobile-xr-evaluation}

The prospective Lighthouse cache study provides a compact example of how an environment turns a study plan into conditional tool execution. It compares 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB capacities while holding the surrounding compute organization, software, and workload fixed. The illustrative background includes an NPU with a $16 \times 16$ array and dual LPDDR5X channels, with the 3\ W budget for the modeled subsystem and a 3\ nm-class process, such as TSMC N3E, as the proposed context (@sec-moonshot). These choices describe one possible study, not a completed Lighthouse implementation.

The environment must turn these candidate requests into tool runs and respond to their returns and failures. @tbl-environment-contract summarizes that behavior. The study is not yet executable: the capacity-to-hardware construction rule, controlled parameters, tool inputs, and measurement procedures still need to be bound; when these prerequisites remain incomplete, the lifecycle mandates an honest stop before dispatch (@sec-architecture-20-ontology). The walkthrough below runs the analytical screen with a real SRAM model and then uses a hypothetical sequence to illustrate the cycle-level execution that follows. It also adds an illustrative analytical screening rule to the study card of @sec-architecture-20-ontology, whose four-execution budget allots one cycle-level trial per capacity plus one rerun; under that rule, a candidate that fails screening leaves its cycle-level trial available to the rest of the budget.

| **Run category** | **Prospective XR subsystem evaluation plan** |
| --- | --- |
| **Candidates and fixed state** | Vary only `l2.capacity` among 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB. Hold the NPU organization, RISC-V cores, memory arbitration, NoC, software binary, XR workload, and cache policies fixed. A specified rule must derive each legal SRAM organization from capacity; capacity alone does not identify its banks, geometry, or macro composition. |
| **Translation and identity** | Prepare analytical SRAM-model inputs and a compatible cycle-level simulation path, such as configured gem5 and Ramulator 2 models. Identify relevant process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions, libraries, wrappers, parsers, tool versions, and seeds. Any Verilator or SCALE-Sim path needs its own representations and supported scope. Power estimates require an identified model or engine, activity inputs, and applicable UPF power intent. |
| **Order and dispatch** | Once prerequisites are bound, perform analytical screening. Admit cycle-level work only when the screening return is complete, matches its schema, and reports area $\le 1.5\text{ mm}^2$ and access time $\le 2.5\text{ ns}$. Passing this screening check permits further evaluation; it does not establish candidate superiority. |
| **Matched work and limits** | Use matched workload and operating conditions for baseline and alternatives. Budget three screening runs and at most four cycle-level attempts, including recovery attempts. Apply specified queue, execution, and study deadlines. RTL synthesis and physical signoff are outside this exploratory budget. |
| **Failures and recovery** | Keep infrastructure failures, tool errors, incomplete returns, and parser failures distinct. Reparse retained material when sufficient; when execution must be retried, create a linked attempt from the required starting state and charge it to the budget. |
| **Containment and reuse** | Restrict each attempt's access to tools and writable paths. Quarantine unconfirmed terminations. Reuse artifacts only when their dependencies and conditions match the intended operation, preserving links to the producing attempts. |
| **Returns, cost, and lineage** | Retain SRAM area, access time, energy and leakage estimates; frame records, memory traffic, and subsystem power with their model and activity assumptions. NPU area and multiply-accumulate (MAC) utilization belong with the relevant NPU model if that path is used. Preserve raw reports, warnings, inputs, outputs, costs, and dependency links. |
| **Decisions left outside** | The harness enforces the supplied dispatch and stopping rules. The method or architect determines measurement validity, comparative conclusions, and whether to advance a candidate or revise the study. |
: **An environment executes the study's rules while retaining their inputs and consequences.** This prospective plan separates preparation, conditional dispatch, recovery, and interpretation; it is not a completed execution specification. {#tbl-environment-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Screening returns for the three Lighthouse capacities: CACTI 7 output written by
# data/run_cacti_lighthouse_l2.py from data/cacti_lighthouse_l2.cfg.in.
_cacti_csv = (
    _root / "book" / "contents" / "chapters" / "06-environments" / "data"
    / "cacti-lighthouse-l2.csv"
)
with open(_cacti_csv, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _cacti = {
        (r["device_type"], int(r["capacity_mib"])): r
        for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#"))
    }
assert len(_cacti) == 6


def _cv(device, mib, col):
    return float(_cacti[(device, mib)][col])


_mibs = (2, 3, 4)
hp_area = [f"{_cv('itrs-hp', m, 'area_mm2'):.1f}" for m in _mibs]
hp_acc = [f"{_cv('itrs-hp', m, 'access_time_ns'):.1f}" for m in _mibs]
lp_acc = [f"{_cv('itrs-lstp', m, 'access_time_ns'):.1f}" for m in _mibs]
hp_leak_w = [f"{_cv('itrs-hp', m, 'leakage_mw') / 1000:.2f}" for m in (2, 4)]
lp_leak_mw = [f"{_cv('itrs-lstp', m, 'leakage_mw'):.1f}" for m in (2, 4)]
assert all(_cv("itrs-hp", m, "area_mm2") > 1.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-lstp", m, "area_mm2") > 1.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-hp", m, "access_time_ns") <= 2.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-lstp", m, "access_time_ns") > 2.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-lstp", m, "access_time_ns") > 2 * _cv("itrs-hp", m, "access_time_ns") for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-hp", m, "leakage_mw") > 1000 * _cv("itrs-lstp", m, "leakage_mw") for m in _mibs)
```

Running CACTI 7 [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI], the analytical SRAM model named in @tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum, on the Lighthouse cache candidates shows why a wrapper must refuse an unsupported technology node rather than silently substituting the closest available one. The pinned CACTI 7 version used here supports characterized nodes down to 22\ nm rather than the 3\ nm-class Lighthouse target, so the wrapper cannot evaluate the requested node directly. If we run the 2, 3, and 4\ MiB candidates at 22\ nm anyway (with 64-byte lines, 16 ways, one bank, and internal array organizations chosen by CACTI's energy-delay-squared objective), high-performance devices return areas of `{python} hp_area[0]`, `{python} hp_area[1]`, and `{python} hp_area[2]`\ mm², access times of `{python} hp_acc[0]`, `{python} hp_acc[1]`, and `{python} hp_acc[2]`\ ns, and standby leakage of `{python} hp_leak_w[0]` to `{python} hp_leak_w[1]`\ W; switching to low-standby-power devices under the same cache specifications shifts access times to `{python} lp_acc[0]` to `{python} lp_acc[2]`\ ns and drops leakage to `{python} lp_leak_mw[0]` to `{python} lp_leak_mw[1]`\ mW. Every 22\ nm area exceeds the $1.5\text{ mm}^2$ target limit, every high-performance access time passes the 2.5\ ns limit, and every low-standby-power access time fails it, yet none of those verdicts answers the 3\ nm design question. The area and latency thresholds were specified for a 3\ nm-class macro, and the unbound choice of device family alone moves access time by more than a factor of two and leakage by more than three orders of magnitude. Following the translation rule above, the wrapper reports the node mismatch as a limitation rather than emitting a screening verdict, and admission waits for a model characterized at the target node (the configuration, script, and parsed returns are retained with the chapter data).

Suppose such a model were available and admitted the 2\ MiB and 3\ MiB candidates while returning the 4\ MiB candidate above a limit. That candidate would receive no cycle-level dispatch under this plan. Its screening result would remain available for review; the screening check alone would not prove physical infeasibility.

One hypothetical sequence then uses the four-attempt budget as follows:

1. The 2\ MiB baseline completes a cycle-level evaluation.
2. The 3\ MiB attempt encounters a setup failure and returns no usable cycle-level result.
3. After the setup problem is repaired, a linked retry of the same 3\ MiB candidate completes under the intended conditions.
4. A repeat of the 3\ MiB evaluation consumes the final attempt.

Reading the record afterward, we find four attempts but only three completed cycle-level evaluations. The failed attempt retains its diagnostics and cost, and the retry remains distinguishable from the planned repeat. This sequence illustrates accounting, not a sufficient statistical comparison: the method must decide whether the retained observations support its intended conclusion. The environment's contribution is an inspectable account of what was admitted, what ran, what returned, and what remains unresolved; whether a clean return actually qualifies the candidate is the question @sec-feedback-verification-trust takes up.

## Open Questions

The chapter describes how to organize tool execution and preserve its history, but it does not settle how much an environment can establish about that execution, at what cost, or how far its results remain useful as designs change.

- **How can a harness verify which requested checks a tool performed?** A clean exit and a parseable report may leave requested corners or analysis stages unaccounted for. Complete logs can expose omissions, but an opaque tool may not report enough to establish which operations it actually performed. The open problem is how to detect missing work reliably across tools and changing interfaces without independently repeating the entire analysis. This concerns execution of the requested checks; whether those checks adequately address effects such as voltage droop[^fn-voltage-droop-c06] remains a separate question of evaluation validity.

[^fn-voltage-droop-c06]: **Voltage droop**: A temporary decrease in supply voltage, which can occur when switching activity changes the current drawn from the power delivery network. It can change cell delays; assessing its timing consequences requires voltage assumptions or analyses that cover the relevant variation.

- **How can an environment verify the required starting state without fully reinitializing a testbed?** Hardware emulation may retain state in external memory, peripheral registers, or host-side processes. Some state is intentionally preserved for checkpoint continuation; other state can contaminate the next evaluation. A soft reset or bitstream reload does not by itself distinguish the two. The unresolved problem is how to establish that all state relevant to the requested evaluation has been restored or deliberately retained, without making initialization more expensive than the work it enables.

- **Which work remains applicable after a design or toolchain change?** A synthesis or emulation run may still be evaluating a fixed revision when an RTL interface or compiler pass changes. Its result remains part of that revision's history, but using it for the revised design requires more than matching an unchanged module name. Dependency graphs identify affected paths only within their recorded assumptions, and local edits can have wider physical consequences. The open problem is how to determine what must be repeated and what can transfer, while preserving useful ongoing work and the evidence needed to justify reuse.

## Summary

An execution environment connects design methods to the tools that construct and evaluate candidates, where its interfaces define the available actions, including whether a method can submit a new implementation or only adjust existing parameters. Whereas setup establishes those interfaces, evaluation paths, and ways to identify their inputs, runtime manages the resulting work as it waits, executes, fails, or resumes so that returned observations can guide further design work with enough execution history to determine what each result describes.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Interfaces define the available design actions.** Specify what a method may inspect, submit, change, and evaluate. Wrappers translate those requests into tool inputs and return structured results without silently changing the candidate or its conditions.
- **Tool choice follows the property being evaluated.** Behavioral checks, timing models, formal analyses, and physical implementation answer different questions. Preserve each path's assumptions, scope, and units when combining their outputs, and expect staged evaluation to reach physical and formal checks once automated work may change structure.
- **Every execution attempt needs its own record.** Link requests to backend jobs, outputs, failures, and costs. Distinguish duplicate submissions from deliberate retries, enforce admission limits so proposals do not overwhelm evaluation capacity, and keep raw reports, warnings, and missing values beside the parsed metrics.
- **Recovery and reuse require controlled state.** Isolate writable workspaces, respect data-access restrictions, confirm termination, and manage shared licenses. Reuse an artifact or checkpoint only when it applies to the requested operation; a matching identifier alone is insufficient.
- **Repeated execution is part of the evaluation plan.** Budget for variation, retain recipes, seeds, and settings, and distinguish randomness from host interference and parallel nondeterminism. A cached result is an existing observation, not a new repeat.
:::

The next step is to decide what these observations support and how they should change the design process. @sec-feedback-verification-trust connects verification, feedback, and learning to that decision.
